levels.title: Base
levels.purpose: Safe, accurate product knowledge and correct everyday knife use.

modules.title: Safety & Control
modules.summary: Build predictable habits before speed: stable workstation, stable food, correct tool, controlled force and safe handling.

content.lead: Many knife accidents begin before the blade touches food.
points: Keep the cutting path clear and the work area dry and well lit.
Dry hands and handle, stabilize the food, choose the correct knife, then identify the blade path.
content.takeaway: Stable board. Stable food. Clear path. Hidden fingertips.

question.prompt: What should happen before the first cut?

options.text: Start slowly and stabilize the board only if it moves.
Stabilize the board and food, clear the blade path, then choose and position the knife.
Hold the food firmly and use extra downward pressure.
Wet the board so the knife cannot bounce.

question.explanation: Safety starts before cutting. The board, ingredient and cutting path must already be controlled.

recovery_questions.prompt: The board moves slightly when you begin slicing. What is the correct response?

options.text: Grip the knife more tightly.
Stop and stabilize the board before continuing.
Use shorter, faster strokes.
Move the food closer to the board edge.

recovery_questions.explanation: A moving board makes every later movement less predictable. Correct the workstation first.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which check best matches the Academy safety rule?

options.text: Sharp knife, fast cut, strong grip, clean board.
Stable board, stable food, clear path, hidden fingertips.
Heavy knife, dry food, straight edge, wide stance.
Large board, soft steel, slow cut, open fingertips.

recovery_questions.explanation: The four-part rule is a compact pre-cut check, not a performance technique.

content.lead: Round and irregular ingredients can move under the blade.
points: Create a flat surface on round produce before the main cuts.
Divide large or irregular food into manageable sections.
Do not force a fine kitchen knife into unsuitable frozen food.
content.takeaway: If the ingredient can roll, the cut is not ready to begin.

question.prompt: What is the safest first action with a round potato that rolls on the board?

options.text: Hold it harder with the fingertips.
Use a heavier knife.
Create a flat face and place that face on the board.
Start with the tip and increase speed.

question.explanation: A flat face turns an unstable ingredient into a predictable one before the main cutting starts.

recovery_questions.prompt: A large irregular vegetable cannot be held securely. What should you do?

options.text: Use more force so the knife finishes in one stroke.
Divide it into manageable, stable sections before continuing.
Change to a flexible knife.
Support it with fingers directly in the cutting line.

recovery_questions.explanation: The geometry of the task should be made stable before adding force.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is a flat base useful on an onion, melon or potato?

options.text: It makes the steel harder.
It reduces food adhesion.
It reduces rolling and makes the cutting path more predictable.
It allows sideways scraping.

recovery_questions.explanation: The goal is mechanical stability, not cutting speed.

lessons.title: Use the right knife and avoid lateral stress

content.lead: A knife can be strong in the intended cutting direction and vulnerable to twisting or levering.
points: Do not use kitchen knives as pry bars, screwdrivers, can openers or levers.
Do not twist a blade free when it binds in dense food.
Do not scrape the board sideways with the cutting edge; use the spine, blade face or a bench scraper.
content.takeaway: Choose geometry for the task and keep load aligned with the cut.

question.prompt: A thin hard blade becomes stuck in dense food. What is the correct action?

options.text: Twist the handle gently until the food opens.
Strike the spine with the free hand.
Withdraw it carefully and adjust the cut.
Push sideways with the blade face.

question.explanation: Twisting creates lateral stress. Withdraw and change the cut instead of levering the blade.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which use is inappropriate for a fine kitchen knife?

options.text: Slicing boneless meat.
Cutting vegetables on a suitable board.
Prying apart two frozen objects.
Drawing through herbs with controlled technique.

recovery_questions.explanation: A kitchen knife is a cutting tool, not a lever.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why should the cutting edge not be used to scrape food sideways across the board?

options.text: It can expose the edge to damaging lateral load.
It makes the knife too warm.
It removes the Damascus pattern.
It changes the handle balance permanently.

recovery_questions.explanation: Sideways scraping loads the fine apex in a direction it is not designed to take.

lessons.title: Set the supporting hand and use only necessary force

content.lead: Control comes from hand position and deliberate movement, not from squeezing harder.
points: Set the supporting hand before moving the knife.
Keep fingertips outside the cutting path; the claw grip is a moving guide, not a speed trick.
If a well-sharpened knife needs excessive force, stop and identify the cause.
content.takeaway: Set the hand first, then move the knife.

question.prompt: A sharp knife suddenly seems to require excessive force. What should you do?

options.text: Increase downward pressure to finish the cut.
Stop and check the edge, food stability, knife choice and movement.
Move the supporting hand closer to the edge.
Use a faster rocking motion regardless of knife profile.

question.explanation: Unexpected resistance is information. Diagnose the cause rather than compensating with force.

recovery_questions.prompt: When should the supporting hand be positioned?

options.text: After the first cut shows where the blade will travel.
Before the knife starts moving.
Only for very small ingredients.
Only when using a pinch grip.

recovery_questions.explanation: The supporting hand defines a safe path before the blade moves.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does excessive force most often tell you?

options.text: The cut should be made faster.
Something about edge condition, stability, knife choice or technique should be checked.
The handle material is wrong.
The knife needs a thicker Damascus pattern.

recovery_questions.explanation: Force is not the default solution to a cut that is behaving incorrectly.

lessons.title: Control the knife when cutting stops

content.lead: Safe habits continue during washing, passing and carrying.
points: Never leave a knife hidden under soapy water or mixed with objects in a sink.
Pass a knife deliberately with the handle oriented to the receiver and the edge clear of fingers.
For short movement, keep the knife low, close to the body, still and with the tip toward the floor.
content.takeaway: A knife must remain visible, controlled and predictable even when it is not cutting.

options.text: Washing one knife at a time while keeping the edge visible.
Carrying a knife low and still for a short distance.
Leaving a sharp knife hidden under soapy water in the sink.
Presenting the handle toward the person receiving the knife.

question.explanation: A hidden blade can injure someone who reaches into the sink without seeing it.

recovery_questions.prompt: How should a knife be carried a short distance in the kitchen?

options.text: Upright at chest height so others can see it.
Low, close to the body, still, with the tip toward the floor.
Flat on the open palm while walking.
Inside a towel held in the free hand.

recovery_questions.explanation: Low and still movement makes the knife path easier for others to predict.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the key principle when washing a knife?

options.text: Keep the blade visible and its edge path controlled.
Soak it first so food releases by itself.
Wrap the sponge around the edge.
Place it with the other utensils before drying.

recovery_questions.explanation: Visibility and control matter more than speed during cleaning.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is the best preparation before cutting?

options.text: Choose knife → cut a test slice → stabilize food if needed.
Stabilize board → clear area → dry hands/handle → stabilize food → choose knife → identify blade path.
Stabilize food → sharpen knife → increase force → clear scraps later.
Choose the heaviest knife → wet board → hold food tightly.

questions.explanation: The complete sequence removes instability before the blade moves.

questions.prompt: A round ingredient rolls easily. What makes the task safer?

options.text: A flat supporting face.
A faster first cut.
A narrower board.
More fingertip pressure.

questions.explanation: A flat face mechanically stabilizes the ingredient.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a blade binds?

options.text: Twist gently.
Lever sideways.
Withdraw and adjust the cut.
Strike the handle.

questions.explanation: Avoid lateral stress; change the cut instead.

questions.prompt: What is the correct relationship between the supporting hand and knife movement?

options.text: Move together from the start.
Set the supporting hand first, then move the knife.
The supporting hand follows the knife.
Hand position matters only at professional speed.

questions.explanation: Hand placement establishes the safe path before movement.

questions.prompt: Which rule remains valid after cutting is finished?

options.text: Keep the knife visible and controlled during washing, passing and carrying.
A knife is safe once it is no longer moving.
The sink is the safest temporary storage place.
Carry the knife high so the blade can be seen.

questions.explanation: Non-cutting handling still requires predictable control.
